events.credibility_reason: Talk abstract seen only in snippets; no written argument and speaker unconfirmed.

Several F10 signals together: a claimed full resolution of a Hilbert problem posted only to Zenodo (no review) with zero engagement or citation after ~9 months; grandiose framing ('paradigm shift', 'restores formal decidability') rather than a stated theorem; an internally inconsistent abstract (claims 'all remaining aspects' while asserting the integer-point version is undecidable, and refers to fixes to 'previous versions' that do not exist); the advertised rational-point decision is classical Hasse–Minkowski with nothing new identified; and closely parallel abstracts on other Hilbert problems (13th, 21st) on the same platforms.

events.ai_basis: systematic collaboration with Claude Code (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI)

why: The statement as worded asks to classify quadratic forms over algebraic number fields; Hasse's 1924 Crelle paper gives exactly that (equivalence over K iff equivalence at all completions, with local invariants), published in a journal of record and universally accepted, so it is whole/digested before the snapshot. Hasse 1921 is the Q case. The integral/representation work (Kneser, Hsia, Duke–Schulze-Pillot, CPS, Blomer–Harcos) answers Hilbert's original integral question, which the bullet does not ask, so it is variant; the universality and generalised-form papers are variant too, and the talks are none. The only post-snapshot claim to the whole, Liu's Zenodo preprint, is scored whole/unreviewed but not_credible on several concurrent F10 signals (see its reason), and in any case adds nothing beyond Hasse for the literal bullet. Swaminathan is a different problem; its AI role is recorded as assisted from the abstract's statement that the proof was developed with an AI-assisted workflow, but the event is a variant and cannot affect this problem.
doubts: If the bullet is read as Hilbert's full 1900 question (integral representation), Hasse 1924 would be a case and CPS/Duke–Schulze-Pillot cases too, leaving the problem partially open; I followed the bullet's literal wording. Hasse 1924's exact statement was seen only via Wikipedia and snippets. Liu's PDF was never read, so its AI disclosure and actual theorems are unknown. Swaminathan's AI quote is thin; assisted vs none is a close call but immaterial here.
